title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 32a -- Interventions: training a baseline model
titleZh: 从零开始编写 LLM，第 32a 篇——干预：训练基线模型
shortTitle: part 32a -- Interventions: training a baseline model
summary: I want to try a bunch of interventions like gradient clipping and removing dropout to see if my models get better. I need a baseline train without them so that I can be sure of the results.
summaryZh: 我想尝试梯度裁剪、移除随机失活等一系列干预，看看模型是否会变得更好。我需要先进行一次不包含这些干预的基线训练，以确保结果可靠。
markdown:
I'm rounding out my series of posts on [Sebastian Raschka](https://sebastianraschka.com/)'s book "[Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)](https://www.manning.com/books/build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch)" by seeing how I could train the *best* base model I can from scratch on my own hardware. I started by [training one in two days on my RTX 3090](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/12/llm-from-scratch-28-training-a-base-model-from-scratch), and found that while it was a decent little model, it wasn't as good as the original GPT-2 small, either in terms of the loss it got on my test dataset, or in terms of how good it was at following instruction prompts after fine-tuning on them. I decided that I wanted to see what levers I could pull -- dropout, attention weight biases, and so on -- to make it better.

For that, I didn't want to have my PC tied up for days at a time with multiple long training runs, so I [learned how to train faster in the cloud](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-29-ddp-training-a-base-model-in-the-cloud). That led to some [refinements in the prompt-following test I was using](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-30-digging-into-llm-as-a-judge), and I also spent a bit of time on a side quest getting the various models I'd trained [onto Hugging Face Hub](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-31-models-on-hugging-face).

Now it's time to try the various "interventions", as I'll call them -- the levers to pull to see if I can make the model better. This post is to recap what they are, and to describe what I did to establish a baseline model to compare to.

### The interventions

I listed a number of possible interventions at the end of the RTX 3090 post; I'm not going to do them all, but for completeness, here's the full list:

-   The amount of training data. I'm not going to dig into this one; it looks like it does help, but the returns diminish rapidly, so I think that in order to get any serious improvement we'd need to train for much more than two days locally. In the one "extended training" test I did, I managed to get the loss down from 4.167 to 4.135, which was... less-than-inspiring.
-   The number of epochs. I'm going to stick to single-epoch training -- that is, I'll train on a single pass through an amount of non-repeating data chosen to take 48 hours to handle on my local machine.
-   The bias on the Wq, Wk and Wv matrices. This one definitely sounds worth looking into -- easy, as it's just a change to a config flag, and makes the model more like the original GPT-2. I'll give that a go. [Here's the post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32d-interventions-adding-attention-bias)
-   Dropout. I've read that for single-epoch training, dropout doesn't help (which doesn't quite work with [my mental model](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/03/dropout-and-mandatory-vacation) of what it's for, but does sound plausible). Worth a look! [Here's the post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32c-interventions-removing-dropout).
-   The learning rate, and weight decay. The values I've used for these are basically copypasta from the book. I think I should learn to understand these and try to optimise them a bit. I'll post separately on each of them. [Here's the one about the learning rate](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32e-interventions-learning-rate), and [here's the one on weight decay](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/03/llm-from-scratch-32f-interventions-weight-decay).
-   The precision. I'm using [AMP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/amp.html), which means that some calculations are done in 16-bit rather than 32-bit, and calling [`set_float32_matmul_precision`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.set_float32_matmul_precision.html) with `"high"` to let PyTorch choose to use the GPU's tensor cores, which use TF32, a kind of "32-bit float lite" (see the [post on the local train](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/12/llm-from-scratch-28-training-a-base-model-from-scratch) for details). Those both (at least potentially) reduce the precision of the train below what you'd get if you trained with full-fat `float32`. Would reverting that be worth the longer train time? I should probably at least poke at that. [Here's the blog post about it](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/04/llm-from-scratch-32h-interventions-full-fat-float32).
-   The batch size. I've already, in effect, tried playing with that. The different cloud machines I played with had different amounts of per-GPU VRAM, so supported different per-GPU micro-batch sizes. So I wound up trying batch sizes from 512 (the same as the original GPT-2 was trained with) down to 104 in the cloud, plus my local trains with a batch size of 6. I did a rough-and-ready calculation [at the end of the cloud training post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-29-ddp-training-a-base-model-in-the-cloud#the-results) where I estimated that the ideal batch size might be something like 97. So, probably not worth much more investigation.
-   Exploding gradients. In one of my local trains, and in three out of the four cloud trains, I had sudden spikes in both training and validation loss. It generally took quite a bit of training -- maybe 10-15% of training time -- to get back on track after some of these, so we had what could be seen as wasted time in the training runs. Exploding gradients can be fixed by gradient clipping, which is relatively easy to do. Definitely worth investigating! [Here's the post on that](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32b-interventions-gradient-clipping).
-   Weight-tying. We have a feed-forward network acting as the output head of our LLM -- the mapping from the embedding-space outputs from the Transformer layers back into vocab space. But the original GPT-2 just re-used the input token embedding's matrix for that. It seems unlikely that that would be a good thing -- after all, our current setup has a flexibility that the original didn't, as the output embedding space can differ from the input one. But who knows, perhaps with a small model like this, it might help? [Here's the post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/03/llm-from-scratch-32g-interventions-weight-tying).

I've worked through each of those apart from the first two and the batch size (and have retrospectively added links to the list above when I do), trying a train with just that intervention and nothing else, on a cloud machine. Once that's done, I'll bake all of the things that helped into the training loop, and do another local train -- with [gradient accumulation](https://www.hopsworks.ai/dictionary/gradient-accumulation) to make the batch size match the cloud instances'.

The cloud machine size that I decided to use for this was the one that came out the most cost-effective (and due to its VRAM size, had the best loss) in my earlier cloud training test: an 8x A100 machine with 40 GiB VRAM per GPU.

But first, we need a baseline model.

### Why a new baseline?

I've already done a train on an 8x A100 40 GiB machine -- why do we need a new one?

In my cloud training post, I came to the conclusion that the cost in terms of training time of running a periodic validation loop as we trained was not really worth it, at least in this case. Two of the biggest reasons to have validation during training are to work out when you're overfitting on a multi-epoch train, and to see how your model can handle datasets that it has not been trained on.

In a single-epoch train like this, you're not going to overfit -- every sample it sees will be new to it -- and the training loss itself is over samples it's not been trained on at the time it was calculated, for the same reason (though of course it will be trained on them as soon as we do the backward pass starting with that loss).

Of course, it's not perfect -- a big benefit of the validation loss is that it's over the *same* held-back dataset on every run -- and there are arguments for keeping it (albeit, perhaps doing full runs less frequently than I was). But for these experiments, I decided that I'd simply drop it.

I also wanted to introduce a consistent random seed at the start of the training loop. I didn't have that in my cloud trains, and of course if we want to have solid results on whether each intervention really does improve matters, then we need one so that we can be sure they're all starting from the same point.

Both of those meant that I couldn't use the earlier train on the 8x A100 40 GiB machine as a baseline; I'd need a new one, introducing those two changes: no validation during the training run (using training loss as a proxy), and setting a random seed at the start for reproducibility.

So: what was the baseline train going to look like?

### Creating the baseline

The first step was to [strip out the validation code](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/5175b84262a95b0c0353d784ed9bb6161e9ee882) and to replace it with code that just took periodic checkpoints, keeping track of which one had the best average training loss over the period since the previous one. Next, I decided to [plot on the training chart](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/9ed8cfd5ff40cde47c8c49a730f0571285469cf8) that is generated during the run not just the training loss, but also an indicator of the maximum and minimum training loss over all of the steps in that period. Then I [added the random seed](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/6a7e5867f86882050fee058cdf9c5880a0f3fcb1), which I set to 42.

A couple of bugfixes, and we were left with [this version of the code](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/tree/dc341a246c13190409d0158765e340d8292a29ae).

One thing to highlight: in the [`train.json`](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/blob/dc341a246c13190409d0158765e340d8292a29ae/runs/8xa100m40-baseline/train.json) file that specifies the various training parameters, I set the per-GPU micro-batch size to 12 rather than the 13 I'd used on this size of machine earlier. Two reasons for that:

Firstly, I'm going to want to do a local run with gradient accumulation later, using all of the helpful interventions. With gradient accumulation, you do a number of steps with batches that you can fit into your memory, but you don't update the gradients each time. After a number of those, you do one big update based on the accumulated gradients -- hence the name. The full batch is all of those smaller batches taken together.

If I want that to closely match the cloud train, I'll want the accumulated batches to be the same size as each global batch in the cloud.

Now, on my local machine, I can fit a batch of 6 into VRAM. So that means that the full batch needs to be divisible by 6 [1](#fn-1). On the cloud train, with a micro-batch of 13 and 8 GPUs, we had an overall batch size of 104 in the previous train. 104 is not divisible by 6: no joy. But with a micro-batch size of 12, we have an overall batch of 12×8\=96, which means we'd be able to do gradient accumulation and do a parameter update every 96÷6\=16 steps.

Secondly, while my estimate of the ideal overall batch size was based on a rather arbitrary bit of curve-fitting, it did say that 97 was the ideal size. So it could be interesting to see whether it did help!

So, having coded that up and set up the configuration, it was time to run it.

Here's the training chart it came up with:

![Baseline training run on an 8x A100 with 40 GiB/GPU](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-32a-interventions-baseline-model/baseline-training-run-chart.png "Baseline training run on an 8x A100 with 40 GiB/GPU")

Note the loss spikes at around global steps 4,200, 13,000 and 23,000. Those are important, I'll explain why later.

The training run reported this at the end:

`Training complete in 12,243.523 seconds Tokens seen: 3,260,252,160 Throughput: 266,284 tokens/second Final train loss: 3.743`

So it took about 3h24m to train, even less than we expected from the previous cloud experiments' estimates of how long it would take excluding validation. About US$35 in cost.

[Here is the model on Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/gpjt/8xa100m40-baseline).

Let's see how it looks.

### Evals

For these intervention posts, I won't run the instruction-following tests, as they can only be run against a batch of models in one go to get results that [are consistent with each other](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-30-digging-into-llm-as-a-judge).

But the smoke test -- how does it complete the sequence `Every effort moves you` is worthwhile:

`giles@perry:~/Dev/ddp-base-model-from-scratch (main)$ uv run test_smoke.py runs/8xa100m40-baseline/model.json runs/8xa100m40-baseline/checkpoints/best/model.safetensors Every effort moves you in on a good cause. If it doesn’t work you would like to join the`

Looks good! Reasonably coherent.

Now we can find the loss on our held-back test set:

`giles@perry:~/Dev/ddp-base-model-from-scratch (main)$ uv run test_loss.py datasets/ runs/8xa100m40-baseline/model.json runs/8xa100m40-baseline/checkpoints/best/model.safetensors Fetching 4 files: 100%|████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 4/4 [00:00<00:00, 990.57it/s] 100%|█████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 3200/3200 [04:53<00:00, 10.91it/s] Loss against our test dataset: 3.692`

That's a bit worse than the 3.674 we got for the original cloud train. Either the calculations of the optimal batch size I did were not quite right (entirely likely, they were very ad-hoc) or the model weights we started with, given the random seed we're using, just happened to lead us in a slightly worse direction (also plausible). Either way, it's in line with what we expected, and is still better than the test loss of 3.725 that we got with the second-best machine in the cloud comparison post (the 8x H100 80 GiB with a global batch size of 216).

So: we have a solid baseline model -- before we wrap up, let's consider those spikes in the loss that I called out in the training chart.

### The loss spikes

Random spikes in the loss are a Bad Thing, right? Certainly they're a bad thing for a train in general, especially if you don't know for sure what's causing them. But my working assumption has been that they're caused by exploding gradients -- for some specific sample in the dataset, the gradients have gone up to some insanely high value, and we've had a bad update to our parameters as a result. It hasn't completely knocked the model back to its starting point, but it does take some time to recover, so we lose the benefit of some of our training.

If that is the case -- and it's not just something like a batch happening to have stuff that's wildly different to the rest of the training data, or something weird in the optimiser -- then gradient clipping is the solution. I wanted to see if it would help the model quality in general, but of course if we hadn't had any loss spikes in this baseline train it would have been hard to see if that was the case!

So I was very glad to see them here, as if there had been none I would either have had to do a gradient clipping experiment with no real expectation of it helping -- or do another baseline train with a different random seed in the hope that that caused some spikes, which would have cost another US$35.

All in all, it was good to see them there, as it sets us up well for that experiment.

### Wrapping up

So, we've trained a baseline model that we can make changes to -- the interventions I listed at the start -- and get a pretty reliable understanding of whether or not they help the quality of the final model. With that in place, we're in a good position to start running those intervention tests!

Given the loss spike situation in that chart, I think that a solid first one to go for -- even though it was the last in that list at the top of this post -- is gradient clipping. Where are those loss spikes coming from, and if it's exploding gradients, what happens if we limit the damage they do with gradient clipping?

Stay tuned! I've already done the training run for that (while I wrote this one up), so I should be able to post about it tomorrow.

[Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32b-interventions-gradient-clipping).

* * *

1.  Well, you could potentially do something with batches of different sizes, but that would be fiddly. [↩](#fnref-1)

So, probably not worth much more investigation. 批大小。实际上，我已经在试验它了。我尝试的不同云机器每个 GPU 的 VRAM 容量不同，因此支持的每个 GPU 微批大小也不同。最终我在云端尝试了从 512（原始 GPT-2 的训练批大小）到 104 的批大小，此外还在本地用批大小 6 训练过。我在[云端训练文章的末尾](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-29-ddp-training-a-base-model-in-the-cloud#the-results)做了一个粗略估算，认为理想批大小可能约为 97。因此，似乎不值得再深入研究。 - Exploding gradients. In one of my local trains, and in three out of the four cloud trains, I had sudden spikes in both training and validation loss. It generally took quite a bit of training -- maybe 10-15% of training time -- to get back on track after some of these, so we had what could be seen as wasted time in the training runs. Exploding gradients can be fixed by gradient clipping, which is relatively easy to do. Definitely worth investigating! [Here's the post on that](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32b-interventions-gradient-clipping). 梯度爆炸。在我的一次本地训练和四次云端训练中的三次里，训练损失与验证损失都突然出现尖峰。出现这种情况后，通常需要相当长的训练（可能占训练时间的 10–15%）才能恢复正常，因此训练过程中会浪费不少时间。梯度爆炸可以通过梯度裁剪修复，而且实现相对简单。绝对值得研究！[这是相关的文章](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32b-interventions-gradient-clipping)。 - Weight-tying. We have a feed-forward network acting as the output head of our LLM -- the mapping from the embedding-space outputs from the Transformer layers back into vocab space. But the original GPT-2 just re-used the input token embedding's matrix for that. It seems unlikely that that would be a good thing -- after all, our current setup has a flexibility that the original didn't, as the output embedding space can differ from the input one. But who knows, perhaps with a small model like this, it might help? [Here's the post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/03/llm-from-scratch-32g-interventions-weight-tying). 权重共享。我们有一个前馈网络充当大语言模型（LLM）的输出头——从 Transformer 层的嵌入空间输出映射回词汇空间。但原来的 GPT-2 只是重新使用了输入词元嵌入矩阵。这似乎不太可能是一件好事——毕竟，我们当前的设置具有原始设置所没有的灵活性，因为输出嵌入空间可能与输入嵌入空间不同。但谁知道，也许像这样的小模型会有帮助呢？ [这是帖子](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/03/llm-from-scratch-32g-interventions-weight-tying)。 I've worked through each of those apart from the first two and the batch size (and have retrospectively added links to the list above when I do), trying a train with just that intervention and nothing else, on a cloud machine. Once that's done, I'll bake all of the things that helped into the training loop, and do another local train -- with [gradient accumulation](https://www.hopsworks.ai/dictionary/gradient-accumulation) to make the batch size match the cloud instances'. 除了前两项和批大小之外，我已经逐一尝试了这些干预（做完后又把链接补回上面的列表），每次只在云机器上启用该干预而不做其他改动。完成后，我会把所有有帮助的改动整合进训练循环，再在本地训练一次——使用[梯度累积](https://www.hopsworks.ai/dictionary/gradient-accumulation)，让批大小与云端实例一致。 The cloud machine size that I decided to use for this was the one that came out the most cost-effective (and due to its VRAM size, had the best loss) in my earlier cloud training test: an 8x A100 machine with 40 GiB VRAM per GPU. 我决定为此使用的云计算机大小是在我之前的云训练测试中最具成本效益的（并且由于其 VRAM 大小，具有最好的损失）：一台 8x A100 计算机，每个 GPU 具有 40 GiB VRAM。 But first, we need a baseline model. 但首先，我们需要一个基线模型。 ### Why a new baseline? 为什么要制定新的基线？ I've already done a train on an 8x A100 40 GiB machine -- why do we need a new one? 我已经在 8x A100 40 GiB 机器上完成了一次训练——为什么我们需要一台新机器？ In my cloud training post, I came to the conclusion that the cost in terms of training time of running a periodic validation loop as we trained was not really worth it, at least in this case. Two of the biggest reasons to have validation during training are to work out when you're overfitting on a multi-epoch train, and to see how your model can handle datasets that it has not been trained on. 在我的云端训练文章中，我得出结论：在训练过程中定期运行验证循环所付出的时间成本并不划算，至少这次实验如此。训练期间进行验证主要有两个原因：多轮训练时判断何时过拟合，以及观察模型处理未见过的数据集的能力。 In a single-epoch train like this, you're not going to overfit -- every sample it sees will be new to it -- and the training loss itself is over samples it's not been trained on at the time it was calculated, for the same reason (though of course it will be trained on them as soon as we do the backward pass starting with that loss). 像这样的单轮训练不会过拟合——模型看到的每个样本对它来说都是新的——而且训练损失在计算时本来就是针对尚未训练过的样本，因为从该损失开始执行反向传播后，模型才会对这些样本进行训练。 Of course, it's not perfect -- a big benefit of the validation loss is that it's over the *same* held-back dataset on every run -- and there are arguments for keeping it (albeit, perhaps doing full runs less frequently than I was). But for these experiments, I decided that I'd simply drop it. 当然，这并不完美——验证损失的一大好处，是每次运行都在*同一份*留出的数据集上计算——保留它也有道理（不过或许不必像我之前那样每次都完整运行）。但在这些实验中，我决定直接去掉验证。 I also wanted to introduce a consistent random seed at the start of the training loop. I didn't have that in my cloud trains, and of course if we want to have solid results on whether each intervention really does improve matters, then we need one so that we can be sure they're all starting from the same point. 我还想在训练循环开始时引入一个固定的随机种子。云端训练时我没有这样做；如果想可靠地判断每项干预是否真的带来改善，就需要确保所有训练都从同一点开始。 Both of those meant that I couldn't use the earlier train on the 8x A100 40 GiB machine as a baseline; I'd need a new one, introducing those two changes: no validation during the training run (using training loss as a proxy), and setting a random seed at the start for reproducibility. 这两者都意味着我无法使用 8x A100 40 GiB 机器上的早期训练作为基准；我需要一个新的，引入这两个更改：在训练运行期间不进行验证（使用训练损失作为代理），并在开始时设置随机种子以实现可重复性。 So: what was the baseline train going to look like? 那么：基线训练会是什么样子？ ### Creating the baseline 创建基线 The first step was to [strip out the validation code](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/5175b84262a95b0c0353d784ed9bb6161e9ee882) and to replace it with code that just took periodic checkpoints, keeping track of which one had the best average training loss over the period since the previous one. Next, I decided to [plot on the training chart](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/9ed8cfd5ff40cde47c8c49a730f0571285469cf8) that is generated during the run not just the training loss, but also an indicator of the maximum and minimum training loss over all of the steps in that period. Then I [added the random seed](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/6a7e5867f86882050fee058cdf9c5880a0f3fcb1), which I set to 42. 第一步是[删除验证代码](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/5175b84262a95b0c0353d784ed9bb6161e9ee882)，替换为只定期保存检查点、并记录自上一个检查点以来平均训练损失最佳检查点的代码。接着，我决定在运行期间生成的[训练图表](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/9ed8cfd5ff40cde47c8c49a730f0571285469cf8)上，除了训练损失，还绘制该时间段所有步骤的最大和最小训练损失。然后我[加入随机种子](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/commit/6a7e5867f86882050fee058cdf9c5880a0f3fcb1)，设为 42。 A couple of bugfixes, and we were left with [this version of the code](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/tree/dc341a246c13190409d0158765e340d8292a29ae). 修复了一些错误，我们只剩下[这个版本的代码](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/tree/dc341a246c13190409d0158765e340d8292a29ae)。 One thing to highlight: in the [`train.json`](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/blob/dc341a246c13190409d0158765e340d8292a29ae/runs/8xa100m40-baseline/train.json) file that specifies the various training parameters, I set the per-GPU micro-batch size to 12 rather than the 13 I'd used on this size of machine earlier. Two reasons for that: 有一点需要强调：在用于指定各项训练参数的 [`train.json`](https://github.com/gpjt/ddp-base-model-from-scratch/blob/dc341a246c13190409d0158765e340d8292a29ae/runs/8xa100m40-baseline/train.json) 文件中，我把每个 GPU 的微批大小设为 12，而不是之前在这种规模机器上使用的 13。原因有两个： Firstly, I'm going to want to do a local run with gradient accumulation later, using all of the helpful interventions. With gradient accumulation, you do a number of steps with batches that you can fit into your memory, but you don't update the gradients each time. After a number of those, you do one big update based on the accumulated gradients -- hence the name. The full batch is all of those smaller batches taken together. 首先，我想稍后使用所有有用的干预措施对梯度累积进行本地运行。使用梯度累积，您可以使用适合内存的批次执行多个步骤，但不必每次都更新梯度。经过多次更新后，您可以根据累积的梯度进行一次大更新——因此得名。完整批次是所有这些较小批次的总和。 If I want that to closely match the cloud train, I'll want the accumulated batches to be the same size as each global batch in the cloud. 如果我希望它与云端训练紧密匹配，我希望累积的批次与云中每个全局批次的大小相同。 Now, on my local machine, I can fit a batch of 6 into VRAM. So that means that the full batch needs to be divisible by 6 [1](#fn-1). On the cloud train, with a micro-batch of 13 and 8 GPUs, we had an overall batch size of 104 in the previous train. 104 is not divisible by 6: no joy. But with a micro-batch size of 12, we have an overall batch of 12×8\=96, which means we'd be able to do gradient accumulation and do a parameter update every 96÷6\=16 steps. 现在，我的本地机器可以把批大小 6 放进 VRAM。因此完整批次必须能被 6 整除 [1](#fn-1)。之前的云端训练使用每个 GPU 微批大小 13、共 8 个 GPU，总批大小为 104；104 不能被 6 整除，无法进行累积。但微批大小为 12 时，总批大小是 12×8\=96，于是可以进行梯度累积，每 96÷6\=16 步更新一次参数。 Secondly, while my estimate of the ideal overall batch size was based on a rather arbitrary bit of curve-fitting, it did say that 97 was the ideal size. So it could be interesting to see whether it did help! 其次，虽然我对理想总体批大小的估计是基于相当任意的曲线拟合，但它确实表明 97 是理想尺寸。所以看看它是否有帮助可能会很有趣！ So, having coded that up and set up the configuration, it was time to run it. 因此，在编码并设置配置之后，是时候运行了。 Here's the training chart it came up with: 这是它得出的训练图表： ![Baseline training run on an 8x A100 with 40 GiB/GPU](https://www.gilesthomas.com/post-assets/llm-from-scratch-32a-interventions-baseline-model/baseline-training-run-chart.png "Baseline training run on an 8x A100 with 40 GiB/GPU") Note the loss spikes at around global steps 4,200, 13,000 and 23,000. Those are important, I'll explain why later. 注意全局步长 4,200、13,000 和 23,000 处的损失尖峰。这些很重要，稍后我会解释原因。 The training run reported this at the end: 训练运行最后报道了这一点： `Training complete in 12,243.523 seconds Tokens seen: 3,260,252,160 Throughput: 266,284 tokens/second Final train loss: 3.743` So it took about 3h24m to train, even less than we expected from the previous cloud experiments' estimates of how long it would take excluding validation. About US$35 in cost. 训练大约花了 3 小时 24 分钟，比我们根据之前云端实验估算的（不含验证）时间还短。成本约为 35 美元。 [Here is the model on Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/gpjt/8xa100m40-baseline). [这是 Hugging Face Hub 上的模型](https://huggingface.co/gpjt/8xa100m40-baseline)。 Let's see how it looks. 让我们看看它是什么样子的。 ### Evals 评估 For these intervention posts, I won't run the instruction-following tests, as they can only be run against a batch of models in one go to get results that [are consistent with each other](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-30-digging-into-llm-as-a-judge). 对于这些干预帖子，我不会运行遵循指令的测试，因为它们只能一次性针对一批模型进行运行才能得到[彼此一致](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/01/llm-from-scratch-30-digging-into-llm-as-a-judge)的结果。 But the smoke test -- how does it complete the sequence `Every effort moves you` is worthwhile: 但冒烟测试——让模型续写序列 `Every effort moves you`——的结果值得一看： `giles@perry:~/Dev/ddp-base-model-from-scratch (main)$ uv run test_smoke.py runs/8xa100m40-baseline/model.json runs/8xa100m40-baseline/checkpoints/best/model.safetensors Every effort moves you in on a good cause. If it doesn’t work you would like to join the` Looks good! Reasonably coherent. 看起来不错！相当连贯。 Now we can find the loss on our held-back test set: 现在我们可以找到我们保留的测试集的损失： `giles@perry:~/Dev/ddp-base-model-from-scratch (main)$ uv run test_loss.py datasets/ runs/8xa100m40-baseline/model.json runs/8xa100m40-baseline/checkpoints/best/model.safetensors Fetching 4 files: 100%|████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 4/4 [00:00<00:00, 990.57it/s] 100%|█████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 3200/3200 [04:53<00:00, 10.91it/s] Loss against our test dataset: 3.692` That's a bit worse than the 3.674 we got for the original cloud train. Either the calculations of the optimal batch size I did were not quite right (entirely likely, they were very ad-hoc) or the model weights we started with, given the random seed we're using, just happened to lead us in a slightly worse direction (also plausible). Either way, it's in line with what we expected, and is still better than the test loss of 3.725 that we got with the second-best machine in the cloud comparison post (the 8x H100 80 GiB with a global batch size of 216). 这比原始云端训练得到的 3.674 稍差。要么我计算的最优批大小不太准确（很有可能，因为计算相当随意），要么是在当前随机种子下，初始模型权重碰巧把训练带向了稍差的方向（这也有可能）。无论如何，结果符合预期，而且仍优于云端对比文章中第二好的机器（8× H100、每个 GPU 80 GiB、全局批大小 216）得到的 3.725 测试损失。 So: we have a solid baseline model -- before we wrap up, let's consider those spikes in the loss that I called out in the training chart. 所以：我们有一个可靠的基线模型——在结束之前，让我们考虑一下我在训练图表中指出的损失峰值。 ### The loss spikes 损失尖峰 Random spikes in the loss are a Bad Thing, right? Certainly they're a bad thing for a train in general, especially if you don't know for sure what's causing them. But my working assumption has been that they're caused by exploding gradients -- for some specific sample in the dataset, the gradients have gone up to some insanely high value, and we've had a bad update to our parameters as a result. It hasn't completely knocked the model back to its starting point, but it does take some time to recover, so we lose the benefit of some of our training. 损失的随机峰值是一件坏事，对吗？当然，总的来说，它们对一次训练来说是一件坏事，特别是如果你不确定是什么原因导致它们的话。但我的工作假设是它们是由梯度爆炸引起的——对于数据集中的某些特定样本，梯度已经上升到一些非常高的值，因此我们对参数的更新很糟糕。它并没有完全让模型回到起点，但确实需要一些时间来恢复，所以我们失去了一些训练的好处。 If that is the case -- and it's not just something like a batch happening to have stuff that's wildly different to the rest of the training data, or something weird in the optimiser -- then gradient clipping is the solution. I wanted to see if it would help the model quality in general, but of course if we hadn't had any loss spikes in this baseline train it would have been hard to see if that was the case! 如果是这种情况，那么梯度裁剪就是解决方案。我想看看它是否会对总体模型质量有所帮助，但当然，如果我们在这个基线训练中没有任何损失尖峰，就很难看出情况是否如此！ So I was very glad to see them here, as if there had been none I would either have had to do a gradient clipping experiment with no real expectation of it helping -- or do another baseline train with a different random seed in the hope that that caused some spikes, which would have cost another US$35. 所以我很高兴在这里看到它们，就好像没有它们一样，我要么不得不做一个梯度裁剪实验，但并不真正期望它有帮助——或者用不同的随机种子做另一个基线训练，希望这会引起一些峰值，这将另外花费 35 美元。 All in all, it was good to see them there, as it sets us up well for that experiment. 总而言之，很高兴在那里看到他们，因为这为我们的实验做好了准备。 ### Wrapping up 总结 So, we've trained a baseline model that we can make changes to -- the interventions I listed at the start -- and get a pretty reliable understanding of whether or not they help the quality of the final model. With that in place, we're in a good position to start running those intervention tests! 因此，我们已经训练出了一个可以继续修改的基线模型——修改的就是开头列出的那些干预——并能较可靠地判断它们是否会提升最终模型质量。有了这个基线，我们就可以开始运行干预测试了！ Given the loss spike situation in that chart, I think that a solid first one to go for -- even though it was the last in that list at the top of this post -- is gradient clipping. Where are those loss spikes coming from, and if it's exploding gradients, what happens if we limit the damage they do with gradient clipping? 考虑到该图表中的损失尖峰情况，我认为第一个可靠的选择 - 尽管它是本文顶部列表中的最后一个 - 是梯度裁剪。那些损失尖峰来自哪里，如果是梯度爆炸，如果我们用梯度裁剪限制它们造成的伤害会发生什么？ Stay tuned! I've already done the training run for that (while I wrote this one up), so I should be able to post about it tomorrow. 敬请关注！我已经为此完成了训练运行（当我写这篇文章时），所以我明天应该可以发布它。 [Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32b-interventions-gradient-clipping). [这是本系列下一篇文章的链接](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2026/02/llm-from-scratch-32b-interventions-gradient-clipping)。 * * * 1. Well, you could potentially do something with batches of different sizes, but that would be fiddly. [↩](#fnref-1) 好吧，您可以对不同大小的批次执行某些操作，但这会很繁琐。 [↩](#fnref-1)
author: Giles Thomas
